This is the one-day course on the EU-frames case with the statistical methods in the foreground, and its centre is the robustness of a published claim. It works on a study of Eurobarometer surveys, which asked whether the economic crisis changed how citizens of the member states frame the European Union, and on a claim of the original author (OA) that five analysts reanalysed in the Multi100 project. Across the day you work as analyst no. 6. You write the estimand behind the claim and finish a causal graph for it. You reproduce, to the third decimal, the result that Multi100 recorded for one of the three analysts whose analyses rest on means of countries or of cells, whichever you choose, and the three reproduced models lead into the methods that a panel of 27 countries needs: fixed effects and random intercepts, the within–between model, and the CR2 test for few clusters. In the afternoon the specification menu is taken apart decision by decision. You explore it and put an exploratory dot on the live class chart, read the chart against the curve of 864 specifications of the claim, and declare one analysis in a shortened preregistration before you run it and submit it as a declared dot.

You leave with an estimand and a causal graph of your own, a reproduced result, two dots on the class chart, one explored and one declared, and the place of your result on the curve of 864. The day assumes that a linear model and its output are not new to you.

## How you work

The day is taught mainly in the browser lab, a page of the course site on which R runs inside your browser, with nothing to install. It works on aggregate data only, the country-year panel of the course and two files that the course rebuilt for two of the analysts, and the lab holds all three; the analyses of respondents belong to the three-day course. Open the lab in a tab of its own and keep this page open beside it. Each part of the day has a page that lists its steps in order, and every step that you work at the keyboard has a button that opens the lab at the right task, or the page on which the work is done. If you have installed R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), the downloadable workspace holds the same tasks and gives the same numbers, and the setup page explains how to install it. The slides are on the [slides page](slides.qmd), and each part opens with a link to its place in the deck.

[Open the browser lab](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"} [Install R and the workspace](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

Several of the steps are things that the class does together, such as everyone typing the value that they have just reproduced and holding it back until the facilitator says go, so the day needs a facilitator. One stretch of the slides is optional, a short tutorial on R in Part 2, and the facilitator switches it on or off to suit the class.

## The parts of the day

- **[Before the day](before.qmd)** (about two and a half hours, more with the installation). You read the case study, the exercise overview and the first sections of the module on statistical methods, fit one model in the browser lab, and read the page on specification curves.
- **[Part 1 – The case and the vocabulary](part-1.qmd)** (ninety minutes). The part sets out the credibility debate, what 'replication' names, and the five analysts of the claim, and it ends with R running on your machine.
- **[Part 2 – The estimand and the causal graph](part-2.qmd)** (ninety minutes, after a break of thirty minutes). You read the paper in full, meet estimands and a short course on causal graphs, and then you write the estimand and finish the graph.
- **[Part 3 – Reproduction and the specification menu](part-3.qmd)** (ninety minutes, after an hour for lunch). You reproduce the result of C6HJR, KQXUE or 018OL, read the three models side by side, meet the problem of few clusters, and work the menu, ending with an exploratory dot on the class chart.
- **[Part 4 – Multiverse and preregistration](part-4.qmd)** (ninety minutes, after a break of thirty minutes). The class reads its chart against the curve of 864, asks what the curve establishes and what it cannot, and each participant declares one analysis before it runs.
- **[After the day](after.qmd)** (as long as you like). The page says where to go next in the companion curriculum.

[Start with Before the day](before.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

The same case is also taught as one-day courses on [open science](../eu-frames-one-day-open-science/index.qmd) and on [data tools](../eu-frames-one-day-data-tools/index.qmd), as a [three-day course](../eu-frames-three-days/index.qmd) that builds the data from the raw survey files, and as a [self-study route](../self-study/index.qmd).
